desc:
An obstacle course has obstacles in a row with heights heights[0..n-1]. For each position i, build the longest possible sequence of obstacles that

  • uses obstacle i as its last element,
  • only uses obstacles at positions 0..i, taken in increasing position order (you may skip obstacles), and
  • has heights in non-decreasing order (equal heights are allowed).

Return an array whose entry i is the length of that longest sequence for position i.
hints: A DP where len[i] = 1 + max(len[j]) over earlier j with heights[j] ≤ heights[i] is O(n²). The goal is O(n log n).
Maintain tails[k]: the smallest possible last height of a non-decreasing sequence of length k + 1 among the obstacles seen so far. This list stays sorted.

For a new height h, find the first position in tails whose value is strictly greater than h (an upper bound). Put h there (or append it); the answer for this position is that index plus one. Equal heights must extend a sequence, which is why it is the upper bound and not the lower bound.
editorial: Process the obstacles left to right while keeping the array tails. If tails[k] is the smallest possible last height of a non-decreasing sequence with k + 1 obstacles, then tails is non-decreasing. A new height h can extend the longest sequence whose last height is ≤ h, so its run length is (the number of entries of tails that are ≤ h) + 1 = bisect_right(tails, h) + 1.

After finding that index k, we write tails[k] = h (replacing the first entry that is larger, or appending when none is larger). That keeps every entry minimal and the list sorted. The index returned by the upper bound plus one is exactly the answer for the current position. Each obstacle costs one binary search: O(n log n) total.
